newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Tensions mount in Bosnian Serb power struggle.
newsitem.headline: Tensions mount in Bosnian Serb power struggle.

text.p: Opponents of Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic said on Sunday they wanted talks with her to defuse a power struggle, but doubts remained over whether the meeting would materialise.
Hardliners said Plavsic and her rival, Momcilo Krajisnik, were scheduled to meet but the president's office declined to confirm that any talks had been agreed.
Political sources said Plavsic was reluctant to meet her rival outside Banja Luka out of fear for her safety.
Senior police officers in Banja Luka have sided with Plavsic since she blew the whistle on alleged corruption linked to the powerful interior minister, Dragan Kijac.
Banja Luka, the largest town in Bosnia's Serb entity, has become Plavsic's power base but hardliners are believed to control the police force elsewhere.
With uncertainty surrounding the meeting, Western envoys said the week-long confrontation may have reached a point where neither side was willing to compromise.
Plavsic was waging a battle against wartime leaders loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic, who she accuses of large-scale corruption.
The United States and European powers have supported Plavsic in her bid to dissolve parliament and call new elections.

Hardliners drew international condemnation when they defied Plavsic and held an assembly session over the weekend. Karadzic's party rewrote laws in a bid to launch a recall vote against Plavsic and to strip her of defence powers.
The NATO-led peace force has stepped up patrols in and around Banja Luka to prevent a possible clash between Plavsic's supporters, which include military police, and Karadzic's security units.
The Bosnian Serb army, demoralised by purges and poor financial support, has vowed to stay out of the dispute but also said it recognised Plavsic as "supreme commander".
Army chief General Pero Colic met Plavsic on Sunday in her Banja Luka offices as nervous policemen stood guard.
Supporters of Plavsic have held large rallies in Banja Luka during the past two days and said they expected a similar demonstration in the eastern town of Bijeljina on Sunday.
U.S. special envoy Robert Gelbard said the conflict in Serb territory would be discussed by members of the NATO alliance at a summit in Madrid on Sunday.
Gelbard issued tough warnings to the hardliners on Saturday, saying the interior minister was playing with fire by refusing to reform his police force under terms of the peace treaty.
Diplomats said Western governments were demanding Karadzic's party allow Plavsic access to the official television network or face unspecified consequences.
Mediators were concerned that two rival governments would emerge in the western and eastern halves of Serb territory, one in Banja Luka, and one directed by Karadzic in Pale, outside Sarajevo.

Although Plavsic remains a nationalist ideologue, Western envoys say she has been willing to cooperate with efforts to enforce the Dayton peace accords to win reconstruction aid and end the Serbs' diplomatic isolation.
Karadzic, twice indicted by a U.N. war crimes tribunal, reluctantly stepped down as president last year under international pressure but continues to wield influence.
An American newspaper reported on Sunday that U.S. Special Forces and the CIA had prepared a secret plan to capture Karadzic but President Bill Clinton had not formally approved it.

Quoting U.S. intelligence sources, the Los Angeles Times said the plan was a response to increasing concerns in Washington that Karadzic was a major threat to efforts at buidling a lasting peace in former Yugoslavia.
